ed883da3bd.q: What are the step-by-step requirements to form a Local Improvement District (LID) in Nevada before issuing bonds?
ed883da3bd.a: The process begins with assembling a pre-application package including property overview, facilities to be financed, bond terms, and assessment methodology. Developers must secure 100 percent property owner consent and enter into a Development Financing Agreement (DFA). The DFA must include fully costed infrastructure plans with estimated start and completion dates. Once the DFA and engineer's report are complete, ordinances are drafted and the bond issuance process commences. Nevada LIDs follow a rigid, non-flexible structure modeled on California AB 1315 and AB 15, requiring extensive front-end planning to avoid delays.

ed883da3bd.rq: These are really one-shot transactions, and they're done in true dirt fashion from the outset because of the restriction on the term of the debt.
ks: Nevada LID structures modeled on California AB 1315 and AB 15 Acts, with rigid (non-flexible) assessment and debt term restrictions
100 percent property owner consent required (not 99.5, not 98 percent) for Nevada developer district formation
Minimum 85 percent of bond proceeds must be spendable within a three-year window to maintain project viability
Bond size threshold of $10-15 million: below this, institutional buyers shift to high net worth retail, increasing interest rates and reducing liquidity
Three-year build-out timeline for assessed infrastructure; assessments begin within a specified time and must end within 30 years

bd6a6eab07.q: What is the 100 percent property owner consent requirement for Nevada LID formation, and what happens if developers begin selling to builders during the process?
bd6a6eab07.a: Nevada statute requires 100 percent consent of all property owners to be assessed in order to form a developer district and skip lengthy formation steps. If the developer begins selling to builders or home builders before the DFA is recorded, each new property owner must become a party to formation documents or sign separate owner agreements. This creates logistical challenges—tracking daily sales, requiring specific disclosures to homeowners, and obtaining power of attorney from each buyer. 09e57bd850.q: What preliminary design and cost estimation level is needed before submitting an LID formation application to a Nevada municipality?
09e57bd850.a: Developers should provide preliminary plans and accompanying cost estimates, ideally with early cost feedback from their general contractor. The public works team will conduct a sanity check on overall pricing during their review of the petition and DFA. While final engineering contracts with the GC are not necessary—especially since improvements are often staggered—precision in cost estimation is critical. Over-leveraging property and misjudging costs can lead to excess bond proceeds or shortfalls, so being as realistic as possible from the outset is essential.

0825b8984f.q: How should developers phase bond issuance across multiple development phases in a large master-planned community?
0825b8984f.a: Bond financing should align with phases of development rather than financing all infrastructure at once. Developers must be confident they can spend at least 85 percent of bond proceeds within a three-year window. This approach emerged after the 2008 recession when large one-time LID financings for 12-year buildouts caused problems when development halted mid-cycle and infrastructure remained incomplete. 6e54978984.q: What is a reimbursement resolution in Nevada LID structures, and how does it finance shared infrastructure like arterial roads serving multiple phases?
6e54978984.a: A reimbursement resolution allows the first phase of a project to finance and construct shared infrastructure (like an arterial road) on its own bond proceeds, with an agreement that future phase districts will reimburse the initial phase when those districts form and issue their own bonds.
